4.label: Signals from authority
4.text: Collective behaviour follows the signals communicated by those in authority. Once people learn that honest correction attracts punishment, silence becomes a survival mechanism. Such an environment can look orderly while being internally fragile, because risks and failures stay undisclosed.

5.label: Culture as experience
5.text: Culture is the accumulated experience people have of how the organisation actually works. Conduct, order and service reveal more than formal declarations. Fear reduces participation, narrows imagination and keeps people focused on protection.

6.label: Trait 1 · Minimal Politics
6.text: Most grievances in a senior team have been aired in three corridor conversations before they reach the colleague concerned. Have the conversation with the colleague first, quietly and directly.

6.label: Unprocessed conflict
6.text: Unprocessed conflict (the moment of unfairness, the overlooked contribution, the public criticism) waits for the next pressure point to surface. Creating the conditions to process difficult moments honestly is operational hygiene.

6.label: Trait 2 · Minimal Confusion
6.text: When the stakes are high, role clarity becomes a survival requirement: no overlapping mandates and no ambiguous accountabilities.

7.label: Trust · the foundation
7.text: The leader who keeps commitments that carry no external enforcement builds the trust that survives pressure. People watch what you do with the obligations you could quietly drop.

7.label: Beliefs to actions
7.text: Shared culture emerges when common beliefs become visible behaviours. Communication alone cannot sustain it; practices must reinforce what the community says it values.

7.label: The belief beneath the behaviour
7.text: Sustainable correction happens when the underlying logic changes. Ask what people are doing, and also: what belief is making this behaviour seem reasonable?

8.label: Drift by toleration
8.text: Cultural drift happens through a series of small, unchallenged accommodations: what is tolerated becomes normal. By the time the values have shifted, no one can point to the moment it happened. Act on early drift.

8.label: Broken promises
8.text: A promise to recognise, promote or advocate for someone that is never kept is one of the most damaging trust events in an organisation. Cultures that forget the promises made in high moments breed a cynicism that is hard to reverse. Use this with “Morale declines”.

9.label: Where capability sits
9.text: The loudest, most senior or most publicly celebrated contributors are not necessarily the most critical. Leaders need to understand where indispensable capability actually sits within the system.

10.label: The fruit test
10.text: A team’s actual culture is what it produces consistently: the quality of the work, the way conflict is handled, the speed of follow-through and the treatment of junior staff. List five concrete outputs and behaviours from the last quarter and ask whether they match the culture the team claims.

10.label: Does truth travel?
10.text: In some organisations people say what is safe, meetings perform consensus and difficult feedback never reaches the leader. Test one regular forum: if something were wrong with the strategy, would anyone in the room say so? Start by asking the most junior person to speak first.

11.label: Quiet disengagement
11.text: The common response to a threat from within is suppression. Ask what created the conditions for it, and talk this week with someone whose quiet disengagement has been ignored.

11.label: Emotional fatigue
11.text: Organisations that run in constant urgency, with no predictable rhythms or recovery seasons, produce people who are always bracing for impact. Rhythm gives people the structure to plan, rest and work.

13.label: Fair-weather results
13.text: A culture can look cohesive in the annual survey and fracture under the first serious pressure. Pressure reveals the weakness that was already there. Ask participants to rate the culture as it behaves under pressure.

13.label: Measure from the bottom
13.text: Organisations that measure culture by the experience of their most senior people miss how most people experience it. Ask: how is the newest person experiencing this culture?

15.label: Rituals that outlived their meaning
15.text: Run three questions across one ritual: what value did this protect when it was created? Does it still protect that value? What would protect it now? Redesign the ritual or retire it; doing nothing is how cultures hollow out.

15.label: Reinforcing systems
15.text: Culture regresses quickly when boundaries and reinforcing systems weaken. Commitments cannot rely on moments of enthusiasm; they need systems, expectations, accountability and people willing to intervene when drift appears.

17.label: What leaders tolerate
17.text: Leaders shape culture through what they repeatedly tolerate, celebrate or ignore, as well as through their decisions.

17.label: CFO · Resource fairness
17.text: Leaders lose credibility when they demand sacrifice from others while insulating themselves from its consequences.

17.label: CHRO · Psychological safety
17.text: Leaders who never create genuine safety find that people manage them from a distance, assessing the relational risk before being open. Safety is built in small moments over a long time, and its absence shows up as managed distance.

19.label: Stated issue and real issue
19.text: The surface complaint is often the one that is safe to raise. The real issue, about authority, recognition or influence, is harder to name. Coaching works on the real issue.

19.label: The soft-rebuke window
19.text: Every leader has a private list of things noticed and not addressed. For each, ask whether it is still in the soft-rebuke window or has moved into harder territory. Postponement is its own decision, and its cost compounds.

20.label: A · Own the conversation first
20.text: Credibility is built through consistent personal commitment. The leader who has not decided cannot credibly call others to decide, so make your own commitment explicit before asking for theirs.

20.label: C · Ask for something real
20.text: A leader who keeps compensating for someone’s stuckness relieves their own friction and leaves the person’s will untouched. Ask directly whether they want to move: capability can be resourced, and the desire to change has to come from them.

20.label: I · Say the honest thing
20.text: People defend against accusation and recognise themselves in a mirror. Feedback that triggers self-recognition changes behaviour more than feedback experienced as attack.

22.label: Softening
22.text: A leader who needs approval more than integrity softens difficult realities, avoids necessary confrontation and lets dysfunction continue. Use this with “which did you abandon or soften?”

22.label: The avoided conversation
22.text: Reorganisations, communications drives and new frameworks can multiply as substitutes for the one hard conversation that is actually required. Name it and schedule it.
